Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert

2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion

   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$

4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$

By [F1], coefficient sequences in the displayed weighted square-sum define unique $L^2$ classes, and Fourier truncations converge in the stated $H^s$ norm whenever that sum is finite. The conjugation condition is exactly the real-valued condition. Under the periodic distribution definition in the Definition, testing $\operatorname{div}u$ against $e_{-k}$ gives $i\kappa_k\cdot\widehat u(k)$, so zero distributional divergence implies $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$ for each $k\ne0$. This proves the equivalence and defines the stated real Hilbert coefficient spaces and projections.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of

derivations.claim: The weak-continuity clause is the continuity of all scalar coordinate maps $t\mapsto(u(t),h)_H$ and therefore defines a property of an actual map; it makes no assertion of norm continuity. The Bochner conditions, by contrast, are properties of almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

If $u,v\in C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere, then for each fixed $h\in H$ the continuous scalar function $t\mapsto(u(t)-v(t),h)_H$ vanishes almost everywhere. A continuous scalar function that is nonzero at any point is nonzero on a relative interval of positive measure, including at an endpoint, so this function vanishes everywhere. Taking $h=u(t)-v(t)$ gives $u(t)=v(t)$ for every $t$. Thus a weakly continuous representative, if it exists for a Bochner class, is unique.

Under the Countable Choice convention in [F1], the periodic targets are separable. Consider finite vector Fourier arrays with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, support in $\{|k|_\infty\le N\}$ for an integer $N$, and conjugate symmetry; their associated real polynomials form a countable family. For $H$ and $V$, apply $P_k$ to each coefficient. This preserves conjugate symmetry and gives finite solenoidal arrays; $P_0=I$ retains the mean mode. Given a target field, first truncate its coefficient series in its target norm, then approximate the finitely many coefficients by rational real and imaginary coordinates with the opposite modes paired by conjugation. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

By [F2], it embeds $V$ into the finite product consisting of the zero extension and its three first derivatives in $L^2$ of that cube. Each ambient space is separable by [F4]. Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable: take its countable base of intersections with ambient rational balls and, using [F5], choose one point from each nonempty intersection. Thus $H$ and $V$ are separable.

The $L^2$ and $H^1$ graph inner products make the ambient spaces Hilbert: completeness of $L^2$ and the Sobolev completeness in [F3] give convergence of Cauchy sequences in the function and all derivative coordinates, and the weak-derivative identity passes to the limit against each test. The spaces $H,V$ are closed by their definitions as closures, so they inherit Hilbert structure. The $V$ norm dominates the $H$ norm; since $D_\sigma$ is dense in both closures, the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous with dense image.

Separability of $V$ and density of $D_\sigma$ in $V$ allow Countable Choice to select $d_j\in D_\sigma$ approximating a countable dense subset of $V$ to every rational precision; the selected countable collection is dense in $V$ and, because $D_\sigma$ is also dense in $H$, its linear span is dense in $H$. Apply Gram–Schmidt in $H$ to the selected collection, discarding zero remainders. Each resulting $e_j$ is a finite linear combination of elements of $D_\sigma$, so is still in $D_\sigma$; its span contains every selected $d_j$ after the corresponding finite stage and is therefore dense in $V$ and $H$.

$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$

Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$

Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer

$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Under Countable Choice, each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

Assume Countable Choice and let $V$ be any separable real Hilbert space. Its continuous real-linear dual $V^*$,
with norm $\|\ell\|_{V^*}=\sup_{\|v\|_V\le1}|\ell(v)|$, is a separable real
Hilbert space. The Riesz map
$$J:V\to V^*,\qquad Jw(v)=(w,v)_V$$
is a surjective linear isometry.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

length unit. Let

$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$

Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Under Countable Choice, each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, $u_0\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time
conventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and
Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
$u:[0,\infty)\to H$ such that its restriction to each finite interval is in
$C_w([0,T];H)$ and its Bochner equivalence classes satisfy
$u\in L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$. All clauses
involving $u(t)$ at a specified time, including the initial trace and energy
inequalities, refer to this weakly continuous map. By the uniqueness result in
Weak time continuity and energy spaces, it is the unique weakly continuous
representative of those Bochner classes. It must satisfy $u(0)=u_0$ in $H$,
$\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for
every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field
$\phi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ compactly supported in
time,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It must also satisfy, for every $t\ge0$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$
and there must be a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for
every $s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and every $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
For a matrix field $A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The tensor pairing means $(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$;

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and open, assume the Axiom of
Choice, let $\nu>0$, and let $u_0\in H$ for the bounded closure spaces
defined above when $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. For $\Omega=\varnothing$, use the same closure formulas: $H^1$ is the finite product of scalar $W^{1,2}$ spaces, $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of compactly supported smooth vector fields, $D_\sigma=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}$, and $H,V$ are its $L^2$ and $H_0^1$ closures. Thus $H_0^1=H=V=\{0\}$ in this case. There exists
$$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$$
with $u(0)=u_0$ and $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, satisfying for
every compactly time-supported $C^1$ map $\phi:[0,\infty)\to V$,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It also satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2\quad(t\ge0),$$
and there is a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for every
$s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
The conclusion is a velocity result for the specified unforced closure-space
formulation; it asserts no uniqueness, smoothness, pressure regularity, or
boundary trace beyond membership in $H_0^1$. Here
$(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$ and
$\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$. For a matrix field
$A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. Write $D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $D_0(\Omega)=\{h\in D(\Omega):\int_\Omega h=0\}$. For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

Extend the real-linear supplier $R$ to complex mean-zero tests by $R_{\mathbb C}(h_1+ih_2)=Rh_1+iRh_2$, where $h_1,h_2$ are real. Their integrals both vanish. Real linearity makes this extension complex-linear; applying the supplier bounds to the two parts preserves fixed-support continuity, the same output-support set, and $\operatorname{div}R_{\mathbb C}h=h$. In the rest of the proof $R$ denotes this extension. On $U=(0,\infty)\times\Omega$, $u\in L^2_{\rm loc}$ and $u\otimes u\in L^1_{\rm loc}$. For a compact $K\subset U$, let $p_{m,K}$ be the maximum of the suprema on $K$ of all component derivatives of order at most $m$. The same local estimate $|\int_K f\psi|\le\|f\|_{L^1(K)}p_{0,K}(\psi)$ shows that the regular pairings of $u$ and $u\otimes u$ are continuous on every fixed-support test space, hence are distributions. The residual functional
$$\langle T,\psi\rangle=\int_U\bigl(u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(u\otimes u):\nabla_x\psi+\nu u\cdot\Delta_x\psi\bigr)\,dt\,dx$$
is well-defined and satisfies
$$|\langle T,\psi\rangle|\le C_d\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(K)}+\|u\otimes u\|_{L^1(K)}\bigr)p_{1,K}(\psi)+C_d\nu\|u\|_{L^1(K)}p_{2,K}(\psi)$$
for every test supported in $K$. Thus its absolute value is a seminorm whose restriction to each fixed-support test space is continuous; by the test-function topology in [F4], $T$ is a spacetime distribution. By [F3], this formula is exactly the residual $-\partial_tu-\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nu\Delta u$ of those regular distributions. For a scalar test $\phi(t,x)$ put $\phi_0=\phi-\theta(x)\int_\Omega\phi(t,y)dy$ and define
$$\langle\pi,\phi\rangle=-\langle T,R_x\phi_0\rangle.$$
The map $R$ is applied at each time. The spatial supports of $\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ lie in one compact subset of $\Omega$, since they are contained in the union of the spatial support of $\phi$ and $\operatorname{supp}\theta$. For each time derivative order, $t\mapsto\partial_t^j\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ is continuous in every fixed-support test seminorm. Linearity and continuity of $R$ on that fixed-support space imply that $t\mapsto R\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ is smooth with derivatives $R\partial_t^j\phi_0$; the support condition in [F2] puts all outputs in one compact spatial set. Thus $R_x\phi_0$ is a smooth spacetime test with compact temporal support, and the displayed functional is continuous by the same fixed-support estimate for $T$. It is a distribution.

For a compact smooth vector test $\psi$, $h=\operatorname{div}_x\psi$ has spatial integral zero by coordinate integration, so $h\in D_0(\Omega)$ and $\psi-Rh$ is compactly supported, smooth, and divergence free. By [F1], $\langle T,\psi-Rh\rangle=0$. Moreover,
$$\langle\nabla_x\pi,\psi\rangle=-\langle\pi,h\rangle=\langle T,Rh\rangle=\langle T,\psi\rangle.$$
Substituting the definition of $T$ proves the full distributional momentum equation. The normalization holds because $(a\theta)_0=0$.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ have the same spatial gradient, their difference $q$ has $\nabla_xq=0$. For an arbitrary scalar spacetime test $\phi$, put $a(t)=\int_\Omega\phi(t,x)dx$ and $\phi_0=\phi-a\theta$. Step 1.1 gives a spacetime vector test $R_x\phi_0$ with spatial divergence $\phi_0$. Hence $\langle q,\phi_0\rangle=-\langle\nabla_xq,R_x\phi_0\rangle=0$, and $\langle q,\phi\rangle=\langle q,a\theta\rangle=0$ by the shared normalization. Thus $q=0$, proving uniqueness conditional on [F2].

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

$$u_n(x)=\sin(2\pi n x_1/L)e_2,\qquad u(x)=0.$$
Each $u_n$ has only the Fourier modes $k=\pm ne_1$ and its vector coefficient is perpendicular to $k$, so $u_n\in H$. For a finite trigonometric polynomial $g$, $(u_n,g)_H=0$ for all sufficiently large $n$ because its Fourier support is finite. Approximate an arbitrary $g\in H$ by such polynomials using [F2]; the error is at most $\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$ times the approximation error. Hence $u_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $H$.

The only nonzero entry of $u_n\otimes u_n$ is its $(2,2)$ entry, equal to
$$\sin^2(2\pi n x_1/L)=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos(4\pi n x_1/L).$$
The oscillatory cosine has zero pairing eventually with every finite trigonometric polynomial and its $L^2$ norm is uniformly bounded; density and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore show it converges weakly to zero in $L^2$. Thus $u_n\otimes u_n\rightharpoonup\tfrac12 e_2\otimes e_2$ in $L^2$, while $u\otimes u=0$. This refutes the false statement. These fields are only a functional-analytic witness and are not claimed to solve Navier–Stokes.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the periodic solenoidal
Fourier spaces defined above. Then there
exists a global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$
under the definition above. This is an existence assertion; it asserts no
uniqueness or global smoothness.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, and $T>0$. Let $z_n:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous
finite-Fourier-sum curves such that, for constants $A,B<\infty$,
$$\sup_{n,t}\|z_n(t)\|_H\le A,\qquad \sup_n\int_0^T\|\nabla z_n(t)\|_2^2dt\le B,$$
and for each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ there is $C_k<\infty$ with
$|\widehat z_n(k,t)-\widehat z_n(k,s)|\le C_k|t-s|$ for all $n,s,t$.
Then some subsequence converges uniformly in each Fourier coefficient to
$z\in C_w([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, with
$\sup_t\|z(t)\|_H\le A$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla z\|_2^2dt\le B$; it also
converges strongly to $z$ in $L^2(0,T;H)$ and, after a further subsequence,
strongly in $H$ for almost every $t$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$,
and $u_0\in H$. Let $u:[0,\infty)\to H$ be the map in the Unforced periodic
Leray–Hopf solution definition with data $(\nu,u_0)$, using its unique weakly
continuous representative, Bochner equivalence classes, weak identity, and
initial and restart energy inequalities. Suppose
$v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$ and
$q\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}v=0$ and
$\partial_tv+\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v)+\nabla q=\nu\Delta v$, with
$v(0)=u_0$. Then $u(t)=v(t)$ in $H$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. More generally,
for $D(t)=\|u(t)-v(t)\|_2^2$,
$$D(t)\le D(0)+2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(s)\|_\infty D(s)\,ds.$$
This conditional result does not assert existence of such a smooth pair.
